questions.prompt: Which chamber first receives blood returning from most of the body?
options: Right atrium
Left atrium
Right ventricle
Left ventricle
questions.explanation: The venae cavae return blood from the body to the right atrium. The left atrium receives blood from the lungs.

questions.prompt: Which chamber pumps blood into the aorta?
options: Right ventricle
Left ventricle
Left atrium
Right atrium
questions.explanation: The left ventricle contracts to send blood through the aorta to the body.

questions.prompt: Which structure separates the right and left ventricles?
options: The pericardium
The tricuspid valve
The interventricular septum
The coronary artery
questions.explanation: The septum is the muscular partition between the ventricles. It prevents direct mixing of their blood.

questions.prompt: What is the main function of the atria?
options: To supply oxygen directly to heart muscle
To exchange gases with the air
To pump blood at the highest systemic pressure
To receive blood entering the heart
questions.explanation: The atria receive blood: the right atrium from the body and the left atrium from the lungs.

questions.prompt: Why is the wall of the left ventricle normally thicker than that of the right ventricle?
options: It generates higher pressure to move blood around the body
It stores more oxygen than the right ventricle
It receives blood from both lungs and the body
It contains more valves than the right ventricle
questions.explanation: The left ventricle pumps through systemic circulation, which requires greater pressure than the shorter pulmonary circuit.

questions.prompt: A student points to the lower pointed tip of an intact heart. What is this region called?
options: The aortic arch
The apex
The septum
The vena cava
questions.explanation: The apex is the pointed inferior tip of the heart and is formed mainly by the left ventricle.

questions.prompt: What do the coronary arteries supply?
options: The lungs with air
The left atrium with blood from the lungs
The heart muscle with oxygen and nutrients
The vena cava with oxygenated blood
questions.explanation: Heart muscle needs its own blood supply. Coronary arteries branch from the aorta to supply it.

questions.prompt: In a normal anterior view of a heart, the specimen's right side is where?
options: On the viewer's right
Always on the upper surface
Always at the pointed apex
On the viewer's left
questions.explanation: Anatomical left and right belong to the specimen, as if it were facing the viewer.

questions.prompt: A small opening between the ventricles could allow what to happen?
options: Blood to pass directly between the two ventricles
Air to enter the heart directly from the trachea
All four valves to become coronary arteries
Blood to bypass every chamber of the heart
questions.explanation: A defect in the ventricular septum can allow blood to pass between ventricles. The direction depends on the pressures on each side.

questions.prompt: Why does blood inside the heart chambers not replace the need for coronary arteries?
options: Blood in the chambers contains no oxygen at all
The thick heart muscle requires its own vessel network to supply its cells
Coronary arteries are needed only to keep valves open
The chamber walls contain no living cells
questions.explanation: Diffusion from chamber blood is insufficient to supply the whole thick myocardium; coronary vessels deliver blood to the muscle itself.

questions.prompt: Which vessel carries blood from the right ventricle towards the lungs?
options: The aorta
The pulmonary vein
The pulmonary artery
The vena cava
questions.explanation: The pulmonary trunk leaves the right ventricle and divides into pulmonary arteries leading to the lungs.

questions.prompt: Which vessels return blood from the lungs to the left atrium?
options: Pulmonary arteries
Coronary arteries
The venae cavae
Pulmonary veins
questions.explanation: Pulmonary veins carry oxygen-rich blood from the lungs to the left atrium.

questions.prompt: What defines an artery?
options: It carries blood away from the heart
It always contains oxygen-rich blood
It always has a thinner wall than a vein
It carries blood only to the lungs
questions.explanation: Arteries are defined by direction of flow. Pulmonary arteries carry oxygen-poor blood away from the heart.

questions.prompt: What defines a vein?
options: It always contains oxygen-poor blood
It carries blood towards the heart
It always carries blood at higher pressure than an artery
It is the only place where gases are exchanged
questions.explanation: Veins return blood towards the heart. Pulmonary veins are an important example carrying oxygen-rich blood.

questions.prompt: Which sequence correctly follows blood returning from the body?
options: Vena cava → left atrium → left ventricle → pulmonary artery
Aorta → right ventricle → right atrium → pulmonary vein
Vena cava → right atrium → right ventricle → pulmonary artery
Pulmonary vein → right atrium → left ventricle → aorta
questions.explanation: Blood returning from the body enters the right atrium, passes into the right ventricle and travels towards the lungs.

questions.prompt: Which sequence correctly follows oxygen-rich blood from the lungs to the body?
options: Pulmonary artery → right atrium → left ventricle → aorta
Vena cava → left ventricle → left atrium → aorta
Pulmonary vein → right ventricle → right atrium → aorta
Pulmonary vein → left atrium → left ventricle → aorta
questions.explanation: Oxygen-rich blood returns from the lungs to the left side of the heart, which pumps it into the aorta.

questions.prompt: What does double circulation mean in humans?
options: Blood passes through the heart twice in one complete body–lungs circuit
Each blood vessel carries two separate blood streams
The heart beats twice for every breath
Blood moves through the lungs twice before reaching the heart
questions.explanation: The pulmonary circuit links heart and lungs; the systemic circuit links heart and body. One complete circuit therefore passes through the heart twice.

questions.prompt: Where does most exchange of substances between blood and body cells take place?
options: Inside the aortic valve
Across capillary walls
Across the thick outer wall of an artery
Inside the vena cava only
questions.explanation: Capillaries have very thin walls and form networks close to cells, allowing exchange over short distances.

questions.prompt: A vessel contains oxygen-poor blood and is carrying it away from the heart. Which vessel is it most likely to be?
options: A pulmonary vein
The aorta
A pulmonary artery
A coronary artery
questions.explanation: The pulmonary artery carries oxygen-poor blood away from the right ventricle. Oxygen content alone does not define an artery.

questions.prompt: Why is the blood returning from an active leg usually lower in oxygen than the blood supplied to it?
options: The leg has converted all oxygen into nitrogen
Vein walls destroy oxygen molecules
The leg produces oxygen that remains in the arteries
Leg cells have taken oxygen from the blood for aerobic respiration
questions.explanation: Oxygen diffuses from capillary blood to respiring cells. Returning blood has less oxygen, although it still contains some.

questions.prompt: Which blood component transports most oxygen?
options: Red blood cells
Platelets
White blood cells
Dissolved mineral ions alone
questions.explanation: Haemoglobin in red blood cells binds oxygen and transports most of the oxygen in blood.

questions.prompt: Which protein binds oxygen in red blood cells?
options: Insulin
Haemoglobin
Amylase
Keratin
questions.explanation: Haemoglobin binds oxygen reversibly, loading it in the lungs and releasing it in tissues.

questions.prompt: Which blood components help start clot formation at a damaged vessel?
options: Alveoli
Red blood cells only
Platelets
Heart valves
questions.explanation: Platelets collect at damaged vessels and help trigger clotting, which reduces blood loss.

questions.prompt: What is the main role of white blood cells?
options: Pumping blood around the body
Carrying most oxygen using haemoglobin
Making the blood flow in only one direction
Defence against pathogens
questions.explanation: White blood cells form part of the immune system. Different types engulf pathogens or help make specific immune responses.

questions.prompt: Which substance is normally transported in blood plasma?
options: Dissolved glucose
Only oxygen bound inside haemoglobin
Large pieces of undigested food
Air bubbles from the trachea
questions.explanation: Plasma transports dissolved substances including glucose, hormones, urea and much of the carbon dioxide in blood.

questions.prompt: How does a red blood cell's biconcave shape help oxygen transport?
options: It makes the cell large enough to block capillaries
It increases surface area relative to volume and gives a short diffusion path
It prevents oxygen leaving the cell in tissues
It allows the cell to act as a one-way valve
questions.explanation: The biconcave disc shape provides a high surface-area-to-volume ratio and a short path for diffusion.

questions.prompt: How does the absence of a nucleus in a mature human red blood cell help its transport role?
options: It allows the cell to produce antibodies
It makes the cell divide rapidly in the blood
It leaves more space for haemoglobin
It turns the cell into a platelet
questions.explanation: Mature human red blood cells lack a nucleus, providing more space for oxygen-carrying haemoglobin.

questions.prompt: A person has fewer red blood cells than normal. Which effect is most directly expected?
options: Complete loss of blood clotting
Complete absence of all blood plasma
Inability of the trachea to stay open
Reduced oxygen-carrying capacity of the blood
questions.explanation: Fewer red blood cells usually reduce the amount of haemoglobin available to transport oxygen.

questions.prompt: Which statement about carbon dioxide transport in blood is most accurate?
options: Much is transported in plasma after conversion to hydrogencarbonate ions
All carbon dioxide is carried only by platelets
Carbon dioxide is never present in blood returning from the lungs
All carbon dioxide travels as gas bubbles
questions.explanation: Most carbon dioxide is transported as hydrogencarbonate in plasma, with smaller amounts dissolved or bound to proteins.

questions.prompt: Why do thin capillary walls support exchange without needing blood to leave the vessels?
options: Capillary walls contract to pump every substance into cells
Substances diffuse across the short barrier between plasma and tissue fluid
Red blood cells must normally burst to release their contents
All useful substances are larger than the wall openings
questions.explanation: Thin capillary walls allow exchange with tissue fluid while blood normally stays within the vessel network.

questions.prompt: What is the main function of heart valves?
options: To add oxygen to blood
To make new red blood cells
To reduce backflow of blood
To separate oxygen from carbon dioxide
questions.explanation: Valves open and close in response to pressure differences, helping blood flow in the correct direction.

questions.prompt: Which valve lies between the right atrium and right ventricle?
options: The mitral valve
The aortic valve
The pulmonary valve
The tricuspid valve
questions.explanation: The tricuspid valve guards the right atrioventricular opening.

questions.prompt: Which valve lies between the left atrium and left ventricle?
options: The mitral valve
The tricuspid valve
The pulmonary valve
The aortic valve
questions.explanation: The mitral, or bicuspid, valve lies between the left atrium and left ventricle.

questions.prompt: Where is the aortic valve found?
options: Between the right atrium and right ventricle
Between the left ventricle and aorta
Between the lungs and trachea
Between the left atrium and pulmonary veins
questions.explanation: The aortic semilunar valve is at the outlet of the left ventricle.

questions.prompt: What does the pulmonary valve prevent when it closes?
options: Flow from the right atrium to the right ventricle
Flow through the vena cava towards the heart
Backflow from the pulmonary artery into the right ventricle
Oxygen diffusing from alveoli into blood
questions.explanation: The pulmonary valve guards the right ventricular outlet, resisting backflow from the pulmonary trunk.

questions.prompt: What normally causes an atrioventricular valve to close during ventricular contraction?
options: The lungs pull the valve shut with each breath
The atrial blood becomes oxygen-free
The valve actively pumps blood backwards
Ventricular pressure becomes greater than atrial pressure
questions.explanation: A pressure difference pushes AV valve cusps closed as ventricular pressure rises.

questions.prompt: What is the role of the chordae tendineae?
options: To help prevent AV valve cusps turning back into the atria
To pull semilunar valves open during every heartbeat
To carry blood directly between the ventricles
To replace the septum when it contracts
questions.explanation: The chordae attach AV valve cusps to papillary muscles, helping prevent prolapse during ventricular contraction.

questions.prompt: Why do many veins in the limbs contain valves?
options: To make blood flow away from the heart
To help prevent backflow in low-pressure blood returning to the heart
To exchange oxygen directly with the air
To make their blood pressure higher than in the aorta
questions.explanation: Venous valves help maintain flow towards the heart, especially against gravity; skeletal muscle contractions also help move blood.

questions.prompt: A faulty mitral valve allows blood to flow backwards during left ventricular contraction. Where does that blood go?
options: Into the right atrium directly
Into the trachea
Into the left atrium
Into the vena cava without passing another chamber
questions.explanation: The mitral valve normally closes between left ventricle and left atrium. A leak can send some blood back into the left atrium.

questions.prompt: Why are the thick, elastic walls of large arteries useful?
options: They absorb all oxygen before blood reaches tissues
They allow valves to replace the pumping heart
They prevent any change in vessel diameter
They withstand high pressure and stretch and recoil as blood is pumped
questions.explanation: Arteries carry blood at relatively high pressure. Elastic tissue stretches during pumping and recoils between beats.

questions.prompt: What usually happens to heart rate during exercise?
options: It increases
It immediately falls to zero
It stays exactly the same in every person
It becomes the same as breathing rate
questions.explanation: A faster heart rate helps deliver more oxygen and nutrients to active muscles and remove carbon dioxide.

questions.prompt: What is a pulse?
options: The movement of air through a bronchus
A pressure wave caused by each heartbeat travelling along arteries
A valve opening inside a vein
A red blood cell dividing
questions.explanation: Ventricular contraction produces a pressure wave in the arteries that can be felt as a pulse.

questions.prompt: A student counts 18 pulse beats in 15 seconds. What is the estimated heart rate?
options: 18 beats per minute
36 beats per minute
72 beats per minute
108 beats per minute
questions.explanation: There are four 15-second intervals in one minute: 18 × 4 = 72 beats per minute.

questions.prompt: For a steady resting pulse, why is counting for 60 seconds less sensitive to missing one beat than counting for 15 seconds?
options: A longer count guarantees that every beat will be heard
Pulse rate must always increase during a longer count
A 60-second count removes all differences between people
A one-beat counting error makes a smaller difference to the estimated beats per minute
questions.explanation: Missing one beat in a 15-second count changes the estimate by 4 beats/min when multiplied by four. Missing one beat in a full-minute count changes it by only 1 beat/min. This comparison assumes a steady pulse.

questions.prompt: Why do active muscles need an increased blood supply?
options: Their cells need more oxygen and glucose for energy release
Their cells stop producing carbon dioxide
Their cells no longer need to respire
Their veins must become airways
questions.explanation: Muscle activity increases energy demand. Blood supplies oxygen and glucose for aerobic respiration and removes products such as carbon dioxide.

questions.prompt: What is stroke volume?
options: The number of breaths taken in one minute
The volume of blood pumped by one ventricle per heartbeat
The amount of oxygen in one red blood cell
The total amount of blood in the body
questions.explanation: Stroke volume is the volume ejected by one ventricle with each beat. It is different from heart rate.

questions.prompt: How is cardiac output calculated?
options: Heart rate ÷ stroke volume
Breathing rate × blood glucose concentration
Heart rate × stroke volume
Stroke volume ÷ body temperature
questions.explanation: Cardiac output is the volume pumped by one ventricle each minute, calculated from beats per minute multiplied by volume per beat.

questions.prompt: A heart rate is 80 beats/min and stroke volume is 70 mL/beat. What is cardiac output?
options: 150 mL/min
1.14 mL/min
560 mL/min
5,600 mL/min
questions.explanation: 80 beats/min × 70 mL/beat = 5,600 mL/min, or 5.6 litres per minute.

questions.prompt: During exercise, heart rate rises from 70 to 140 beats/min while stroke volume rises from 60 to 90 mL/beat. What happens to cardiac output?
options: It rises from 4.2 to 12.6 litres/min
It rises from 4.2 to 8.4 litres/min
It falls from 12.6 to 4.2 litres/min
It stays at 6.3 litres/min
questions.explanation: At rest: 70 × 60 = 4,200 mL/min. During exercise: 140 × 90 = 12,600 mL/min. Both rate and stroke volume matter.

questions.prompt: A trained person and an untrained person both have a resting cardiac output of 5 L/min. The trained person has a lower resting heart rate. What follows?
options: The trained person must have no heart valves
The trained person must have a larger stroke volume at that time
The untrained person must have no haemoglobin
Both must have exactly the same stroke volume
questions.explanation: For the same cardiac output, a lower heart rate must be balanced by a larger volume pumped per beat.

questions.prompt: What happens when a coronary artery becomes severely narrowed?
options: More air enters the left atrium
The pulmonary veins turn into arteries
Less blood can reach part of the heart muscle
All red blood cells stop containing haemoglobin
questions.explanation: Narrowing reduces blood supply to heart muscle, limiting its oxygen and nutrient supply.

questions.prompt: What is atherosclerosis?
options: The normal opening of a heart valve
The production of red blood cells in the lungs
The flow of blood through capillaries
The build-up of fatty plaques in artery walls
questions.explanation: Atherosclerosis involves plaque build-up in arterial walls, which can narrow vessels and increase cardiovascular risk.

questions.prompt: Why can a blocked coronary artery cause heart muscle damage?
options: The affected muscle may receive too little oxygen for its energy needs
It makes the heart inhale air instead of blood
It raises the oxygen content of every heart cell
It stops the blood from containing any water
questions.explanation: A blocked coronary artery can starve part of the myocardium of oxygen. Prolonged loss of supply can cause cell death.

questions.prompt: Which change is likely to reduce cardiovascular risk over time?
options: Starting smoking to increase heart rate
Regular appropriate physical activity and avoiding smoking
Replacing all water with highly sugary drinks
Remaining inactive to avoid using the heart
questions.explanation: Regular activity and avoiding smoking are evidence-based ways to lower cardiovascular risk, alongside other healthy habits.

questions.prompt: Why is high blood pressure a risk factor for cardiovascular disease?
options: It ensures every artery is completely free of plaque
It means the lungs contain too much oxygen
It places extra strain on vessels and the heart over time
It makes all heart valves work without pressure differences
questions.explanation: Persistently high blood pressure can damage vessel walls and increases the workload of the heart.

questions.prompt: A class investigates the effect of exercise duration on pulse rate. Which variable should they change?
options: The method of counting pulse for every trial
The measurement interval at random
The exercise type and duration together
The duration of the exercise
questions.explanation: The independent variable is exercise duration. Keeping other important conditions similar helps isolate its effect.

questions.prompt: In an investigation comparing pulse rates after the same exercise, why should the delay before counting be kept similar?
options: Heart rate can fall during recovery, so different delays affect the comparison
Pulse rate never changes after exercise
The heart produces no pulse during recovery
A longer delay always means a higher pulse rate
questions.explanation: Heart rate often decreases as recovery proceeds. Standardising the measurement delay makes results more comparable.

questions.prompt: Why is it useful to repeat pulse measurements and calculate a mean?
options: It guarantees that there are no systematic errors
It reduces the influence of random variation in individual measurements
It makes an unfair method automatically fair
It proves the same result applies to every person
questions.explanation: Repeats and a mean reduce the influence of random variation. They do not remove a consistently biased measurement method.

questions.prompt: A student finds a lower resting pulse after several weeks of training. What is the strongest conclusion from this observation alone?
options: Training has proved that all heart disease has been prevented
Every other student must have had the same change
The resting pulse was lower in the later measurement, but other factors should be considered
The student's blood no longer needs to carry oxygen
questions.explanation: One observation shows a change, but fitness, stress, temperature, illness and measurement conditions can all influence pulse.

questions.prompt: Two groups do different exercises and compare raw pulse counts collected over different time intervals, without converting them to beats per minute. Why is the comparison difficult to interpret?
options: All exercise must produce exactly the same pulse rate
Pulse rate cannot ever be measured in school
Different counting intervals always give identical raw counts
Both exercise and counting duration differ, so raw counts cannot isolate the effect of exercise
questions.explanation: A raw count depends on pulse rate and counting duration. Convert counts to beats per minute and standardise other important conditions so that the comparison can isolate the intended exercise variable.
